topic.angle: The ice cream and drowning example

card.title: Ice cream and drowning rise together

body.claim: Two things can rise together without one causing the other.
body.why: As ice cream sales rise, so do drowning deaths, but ice cream does not cause drowning. The example misses the time of year and temperature, which are linked to ice cream sales. A hidden factor that affects both things is called a confounding (or lurking) variable.

probes.question: Ice cream sales and drownings rise together. Which explanation fits best?
options: Drowning makes people buy ice cream
Something else, like hot weather, is linked to both
Nothing can be concluded about any link, ever

probes.question: True or false: a confounding variable is a third factor that affects both of the things being compared.

image_brief.show: File:Ice cream cone at the beach.jpg shows a hand holding an ice cream cone at a beach

claims.claim: As ice cream sales rise, so do drowning deaths
claims.quote: As ice cream sales increase, the rate of drowning deaths increases sharply.

claims.claim: The example misses time of year and temperature, linked to ice cream sales
claims.quote: This example fails to recognize the importance of time of year and temperature to ice cream sales.

claims.claim: Hot weather is linked to both (probe)
claims.quote: Ice cream is sold during the hot summer months at a much greater rate than during colder times

claims.claim: Hidden factor affecting both is a lurking variable
claims.quote: a hidden third variable that affects both of the variables observed to be correlated

claims.claim: Also known as a confounding variable
claims.quote: That third variable is also known as a confounding variable
claims.note: Page notes confounding variables need not be hidden; card's '(or lurking)' is acceptable.
